title: King's Handwritten Speech Draft Goes on Show for the First Time
summary:
The only known draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s famous 1963 speech is on show for the first time. The seven-page handwritten draft is on display at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, through Sunday.

It is written in cursive, in blue ink on yellow legal paper. King crossed out parts and reworked them. Jill Savitt, the center's CEO, said it shows King wrestling with the words.

King first titled it "Normalcy Never Again." But the draft lacks the famous words "I Have a Dream." King improvised them on August 28, 1963, before 250,000 people on the National Mall.

Xernona Clayton, an Atlanta leader, found the papers in a manila envelope in her husband's desk in the late 1990s. Now 96, she rediscovered them recently and decided to share them. Her husband, Edward Clayton, was one of King's speechwriters.

The manuscript will be auctioned through Christie's in January, where bids could top $10 million. It will also be shown in Chicago. Shirley Franklin visited last week and said she sat by the reflecting pool.
why_it_matters: Seeing how King changed and reworked his words can help you keep improving your own writing until it says just what you mean.

keywords.explanation: A manuscript is a piece of writing done by hand, not printed.
Cursive is a style of handwriting where the letters are joined together.
To improvise is to make something up on the spot without planning it first.
Speechwriters are people who help write speeches for someone else.
When something is auctioned, people offer money for it and the highest offer wins it.
